title: Do You Realize How Hard It Is
author: Summer Mulder
summary: A vendor booking at a country music festival becomes the occasion for Mulder's argument about the unglamorous middle of any ambitious project. Two relatively unknown performers, playing to a crowd that did not know their songs, gave everything anyway, and one admitted from the stage that he was not sure he had enough gas money to get home. Mulder treats this as the hardest thing a person can do, performing fully in the part of the journey where it hurts, where it is lonely and where you doubt yourself as much as others doubt you. She generalises from the anecdote to anyone who stands back up after a loss and pours themselves into something with no guarantee of return, arguing this is a different category from working hard. Her claim is that this particular pain is formative, the place where a person becomes hard to break, not because it stops hurting but because the dream outweighs it. The essay then answers the well-meaning question of why not settle for what you already have, insisting that continued striving comes from fullness rather than emptiness and is itself a form of gratitude. She closes by revisiting her earlier question about addiction to struggle, suggesting instead that each level of growth reveals a higher one that cannot be unseen.
points: Mulder's admiration is explicitly for the unrecognised performers rather than the headliners, which sets up her argument that character is formed in the middle rather than at the top.
The detail that one artist was unsure he had gas money home while performing as though opening for a king is the essay's evidence, not decoration.
She distinguishes ordinary hard work from the specific fight of continuing when the spirit is heavy and there is no guarantee of payoff.
The answer she gives to well-meaning people who ask whether it is enough reframes striving as gratitude and fullness rather than emptiness or ingratitude.
Her revision of her own earlier framing is the most interesting turn: not addiction to struggle, but the impossibility of unseeing a higher vantage point once growth has revealed it.
quotes: They walked on stage, relatively unknown, and performed like the whole world was watching.
To be in the middle of your journey, not at the top, not at the glamorous highlight reel moment, but in the grit.
In fact, one shared that he wasn’t even quite sure he had enough gas to make it home. Yet, there he was on the big stage, guitar in hand, singing like he was opening for the king.
And yet somehow, you stand back up. You show up. You pour your soul into something with no guarantee that it’s ever going to pay off.
That’s where something changes in you. That’s where you become someone who cannot be broken.
No, we’re not chasing this because we’re empty. We’re chasing this because we’re full… full of potential, of ideas, of this wild urge to do the thing we know we can, while we still have time here.
And maybe… maybe it’s not that we’re addicted to the struggle. Maybe it’s that with every level of growth, we can see higher. And once you’ve seen higher, it’s really damn hard to unsee it.
